gaps.title: Deploying defense takes trucks, crews and setup time
gaps.problem: Most systems arrive on a vehicle, need a site built around them, and need a trained operator to aim, fly or monitor them. In a fast-moving fight, or at a base that has nothing installed, that is time and people nobody has.

evidence.text: L3Harris's VAMPIRE counter-drone kit takes about two hours and two people to install.
The Army's main counter-drone radar (KuMRFS) deploys in about 30 minutes, at a site or on a vehicle.
JIATF-401's director wants installations to set up counter-drone gear "like a Ring doorbell," without vendor technicians.
Trained operators are the bottleneck: about 60 US police officers held counter-drone mitigation certification by June 2026, out of 18,500+ agencies.
Ukraine's president said its interceptors have already outnumbered its trained operators.

gaps.fit_note: This is UM's main advantage: one soldier carries the canister, launches it, and goes back to the mission while the interceptor's own sensors do the work.

gaps.title: Jammers can't stop a drone that isn't transmitting
gaps.problem: The most common defenses jam or hijack the radio link. A drone flying a pre-programmed route, or simply staying radio-silent, gives them nothing to grab.

evidence.text: The first approved technology list for US police counter-drone work is expected to be radio-frequency only: detection, jamming and takeover.
NORTHCOM's response to drones over a strategic US base in the first hours of the Iran war was jamming.
Cartels on the southern border keep changing tactics to avoid detection.

gaps.fit_note: UM's onboard radar and EO/IR camera track the drone itself, so it doesn't matter whether the target is transmitting.

gaps.title: The strongest weapons can't be used over US towns
gaps.problem: Guns, missiles, lasers and microwave weapons work overseas, but falling rounds, debris and beams over neighborhoods, airports and stadiums are not acceptable at home.

evidence.text: NORTHCOM said lasers, microwave weapons, missiles and guns are not appropriate for homeland drone defense.
A counter-drone laser fired near Fort Bliss shut El Paso's airspace for more than seven hours in February 2026.
JIATF-401 has asked for kinetic interceptors without explosive warheads for homeland use.
The Pentagon's first Replicator 2 purchase was a net-capture interceptor, picked because capture avoids collateral damage at home.

gaps.fit_note: UM's first version captures the drone with a tethered rope and brings it down under control: the low-collateral approach buyers are asking for.

gaps.title: Most US bases still have no drone defense
gaps.problem: Coverage is patchy and expensive. Fixed systems cost tens of millions per site, so many installations, including training bases, sit uncovered.

evidence.text: The DoD Inspector General found major bases, including Luke AFB where most F-35 pilots train, without clear counter-drone coverage.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates about $74M to equip one installation with layered defense, plus about $5M a year to run it.
In January 2026 commanders gained authority to engage drones beyond the fence line, which widens the area each base must cover.

gaps.fit_note: A canister system needs no installation, so it can cover a site the day it arrives, or move with the unit.

gaps.title: Defense still costs more than the attack
gaps.problem: Missiles costing $100,000+ are fired at drones costing a few thousand. The new answer is cheap interceptor drones, but most are destroyed on every shot.

evidence.text: The Army pays about $15,000 per Merops interceptor and aims for $3,000–5,000 at scale, against $30,000–50,000 per Shahed.
Ukraine reports needing 2–3 interceptors for each Shahed.

gaps.fit_note: UM is designed to be recovered and flown again. Measuring the recovery rate is how UM turns that into a cost advantage.

fit.headline: Carry it. Launch it. Get back to the mission.
fit.lede: Unified Mechanics builds a drone interceptor that one soldier carries in a canister and launches with no setup. Once it's in the air, its own radar and camera find and track the target, so nobody has to aim it or fly it.

points.title: Ultra-portable
points.text: The interceptor travels and launches from a man-portable canister. No truck, no trailer, no launch pad, no site to build.

points.title: No thought required to deploy
points.text: Onboard radar and EO/IR do the tracking. The soldier launches it and turns back to the mission, with no aiming and no piloting.

points.title: Safe to use at home
points.text: The first version captures the drone with a tethered rope and lowers it under control, the low-collateral approach US buyers are asking for. A kinetic ram follows in later versions.

points.title: Sees drones that stay silent
points.text: Its sensors don't depend on the target transmitting, unlike jammers.

points.title: Comes back
points.text: Designed to be recovered and reused, not destroyed on every shot.

fit.competition_note: Competitors with parts of this: Fortem's DroneHunter captures drones but launches from a fixed pad with a ground radar. Zone 5's Paladin carries its own radar and is low-collateral; it has no published man-portable launch. Origin BLAZE and Askari are man-portable but carry warheads.

steps.title: Get tested where buyers watch
steps.text: The Air Force's Point Defense Battle Lab asked for drone-on-drone interceptors for US bases. The Navy's Thunderdome event sought interceptors under 18 lb, faster than 85 knots and under $25,000, that operate non-kinetically. UM's capture effector is non-kinetic by design, so it fits that profile.

steps.title: Submit to the front door
steps.text: JIATF-401's Commercial Solutions Opening takes solution briefs on a rolling basis through 2028. Its Mobile office is looking for rapidly transportable systems for border defense and special events.

steps.title: Get on the shelf
steps.text: Listing on the Pentagon's counter-drone marketplace (cuas.mil) and the Army's G-TEAD fast lane lets units buy directly. Merops, which the Army bought by the thousand in 2026, was fast-tracked through G-TEAD.

steps.title: Plug into the network
steps.text: Anduril's Lattice is now the Army's counter-drone command system, and a common US-UK data standard is becoming a listing requirement. Integrating with both lets any unit add UM to its existing setup.

steps.title: Scale through the big vehicles
steps.text: Twelve companies now hold slots on JIATF-401's $7B contract and DHS has a $1.5B vehicle. Teaming with holders that lack an airborne interceptor is the route to volume orders at home and abroad.
